memories.content: Complete the problem framing within the first two sentences so the reader reaches the proposal's central issue before any supporting background.
Use the first sentence for the concrete problem and the second for its consequence; reserve later sentences for the proposed response.
Specify the user, context, and interaction to be explored in the primary HCI research question.
Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
Present the master’s research schedule as phased periods for exploration, design, prototyping, and user evaluation.
Link one reviewable deliverable to each phase of the master’s research.
Place the gap left by HCI-related research and the proposed design and empirical contributions in close proximity.
Divide a two-page proposal with short descriptive subheadings so a reader can jump directly to the problem, proposed response, and next steps.
Give the problem and proposed response their own descriptive subheadings instead of relying only on paragraph transitions.
Give the next steps and requested support their own descriptive subheading so they remain easy to find on a return visit.
Place pilot observation or initial prototype results near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
Readers often decide what a proposal is about from its first two sentences before scanning the rest of the page.
When setup continues past the second sentence, readers who are skimming often retain the background topic but miss the exact problem being proposed.
Reuse the same short subheadings in discussion so a reader can return to a section without searching through the whole page.
Use visible subheadings as a completeness check: an empty or missing section makes an omitted part of the proposal immediately apparent.
Readers often scan section labels before deciding which paragraph to read closely.
Calculate user research compensation budgets based on the estimated participation burden, combining session time with required technical and travel preparation.
Compensate participants who withdraw from the study midway for their actual participation time.
Compensate for the time actually spent in sessions, regardless of the research modality.
Allow the issuance of gift cards of equivalent value to participants in remote studies who cannot use electronic transfers.
Do not treat an unresolved payment method as a deficiency at the proposal stage.
Allow differential compensation amounts for on-site and remote studies when participation burden varies due to travel or technical preparation.
Participants judge the fairness of compensation based on the combined burden of session time and required technical and travel preparation.
In longitudinal studies requiring diary entries and repeated reporting, include out-of-session recording time in compensation calculations.
Distinguish between participant research compensation and labor costs for field staff performing installation and operational support as part of their duties.
The user tends to count session time but omit participants’ advance setup and follow-up reporting time.

analysis.overview: The frames address separate operational areas: the reference concentrates on proposal structure, research framing, visual explanation, scheduling, and evidence placement, while the compared frame concentrates on fair participant compensation, payment mechanisms, and cost classification. Neither side supplies a scope-aligned counterpart to the other.

relations.reason: These reference-side memories split one underlying claim into the recommended opening structure and the reader-behavior rationale supporting it; the compared frame contains no compensation-policy counterpart.
relations.summary: The proposal should establish the concrete problem and its consequence within its first two sentences because readers may otherwise miss the central issue while skimming.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-side requirement for research-question specificity, with no counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: The primary HCI research question should identify the user, context, and interaction under study.

relations.reason: The reference-side memories divide one visual-explanation requirement into providing the summary and showing its transition logic; the compared frame contains no corresponding claim.
relations.summary: An unfamiliar interaction procedure should have a compact visual summary that marks the conditions governing transitions between steps.

relations.reason: These reference-side memories split one schedule-planning claim into phase structure and phase-level outputs, without a counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: The master’s research schedule should organize exploration, design, prototyping, and evaluation into phases, each tied to a reviewable deliverable.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-side placement rule, and the compared frame does not address it.
relations.summary: The HCI research gap and the proposed design and empirical contributions should appear near each other.

relations.reason: These reference-side memories elaborate one underlying subheading practice through section coverage and its navigation and completeness benefits; the compared frame contains no corresponding guidance.
relations.summary: A short proposal should use consistent descriptive subheadings for its major parts to support scanning, return navigation, and completeness checking.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-side evidence-placement rule with no counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: Pilot observations or initial prototype results should be placed near the feasibility claims they support.

relations.reason: These compared-side memories develop one underlying total-burden compensation claim through its fairness rationale, common omission, modality implication, and longitudinal application; the reference frame contains no compensation guidance.
relations.summary: Participant compensation should reflect total participation burden, including technical or travel preparation and applicable out-of-session reporting, allowing modality-based differences when burdens differ.

relations.reason: These compared-side memories state one actual-time payment policy and its withdrawal application; the reference frame contains no counterpart.
relations.summary: Participants should be compensated for time actually spent participating, regardless of modality and including partial participation before withdrawal.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful compared-side payment-method alternative, with no counterpart in the reference frame.
relations.summary: Remote-study participants unable to use electronic transfers may receive gift cards of equivalent value.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful compared-side proposal-review rule, distinct from selecting a specific payment alternative and absent from the reference frame.
relations.summary: An unresolved participant payment method should not be treated as a proposal-stage deficiency.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful compared-side cost-classification rule, with no counterpart in the reference frame.
relations.summary: Participant research compensation should be distinguished from labor costs for field staff performing installation and operational support as part of their duties.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame covers burden-based and time-based participant compensation, withdrawal payments, remote payment alternatives, proposal-stage payment-method flexibility, longitudinal reporting time, and separation of participant compensation from staff labor costs.
reports.reference_only: The reference provides proposal-writing guidance on early problem framing, research-question specificity, interaction visuals, phased schedules, gap-and-contribution placement, navigable subheadings, and nearby feasibility evidence.
